name: Royal Arcade, Melbourne
label: Royal Arcade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Little Collins Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Little Collins Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/46865640: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Royal Arcade' (125 m across).
notes: Victorian shopping arcade with Gaunt's clock and mosaic floor.

text.description:
Royal Arcade is a Victorian shopping arcade in the middle of Melbourne's city centre, and it is the oldest surviving arcade in Australia. It opened in 1870 and links Bourke Street Mall with Little Collins Street. Inside, a high glass roof sits on cast iron frames above bow-fronted shops, and the black-and-white chequered floor leads your eye along the whole length. The shopfronts were restored in 2002-04 and painted yellow and white with gilded touches, so the colours photograph warmly.

The best photo is at the Little Collins Street end. Stand just inside the doors, and turn round to look up. There you'll find the carved giants Gog and Magog on either side of Gaunt's Clock, added in 1893. They are based on the figures in London's Guildhall, and they strike bells with their arms each hour. Seen from below, they make a strong, centred shot with the arched niche around them.

If you have time, take a second photo of the long view down the corridor, either from the main entrance on Bourke Street Mall or from further inside the arcade. The roof, shop fronts and floor all lead the eye in the same direction, which makes a tidy, symmetrical picture. Keep moving gently, as it is a through-route for shoppers and walkers.
text.geographic_location: Royal Arcade is in the central business district of Melbourne, running between Bourke Street Mall and Little Collins Street. It sits close to the other Victorian arcade, the Block Arcade, and is part of the city's network of lanes and arcades.
text.directions_text: There is no station or tram stop right at this spot, so head for Bourke Street Mall or Little Collins Street in the city centre. From there the middle of the arcade is about 1 minute on foot to the north. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit both giants, the clock and the arch in one frame. Then try the default lens (1x) for a cleaner view with less distortion. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for a close-up of the clock face or the carved figures.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Little Collins Street (Little Collins Street entrance, just inside the doors, looking up at Gog and Magog and the Gaunt's Clock). The two carved giants Gog and Magog flanking the Gaunt's Clock, seen from below at the arcade's southern entrance. From here the figures and the clock are above you, framed by the arch.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the clock up with the centre line so the two giants sit evenly on each side. Keep the phone level, as tilting it back makes the walls lean inwards. For a second picture, face north and shoot down the corridor, with the glass roof and shop fronts running away from you. The same long view is available from the Bourke Street Mall entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the clock to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright glass roof and sky don't wash out the carvings. Hold the phone with both hands and keep it still; the light inside can be dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around the top of the hour, when the figures strike the bells. Arrive a few minutes early to get your spot and frame.

text.access_note: Royal Arcade is a shopping arcade used as a public walk-through; check the official site before you go for opening times and any access rules.

name: Melbourne Cricket Ground
label: Melbourne Cricket Grou
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Yarra Park' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Yarra Park' (way/131707394): edge nearest the subject (1182 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/210337258: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Melbourne Cricket Ground' (510 m across).
notes: Giant sports stadium in Yarra Park.

text.description:
The Melbourne Cricket Ground, known locally as the 'G, is the largest stadium in Australia, with a capacity of about 100,000. It sits in Yarra Park in East Melbourne. The Melbourne Cricket Club established the ground in 1853, and it is built on what was a Wurundjeri camping ground. It hosted the world's first Test match in 1877, the opening and closing ceremonies of the 1956 Olympics, and today stages the AFL Grand Final and the Boxing Day Test. It is on the Victorian Heritage Register and the Australian National Heritage List.

It photographs well because of its sheer scale. From the park, the floodlights and the tops of the stands rise above the trees, and open lawn and paths give you a clear foreground. A wide shot with grass, trees and stadium layered together shows the size of the place better than a close-up of one wall. Use the paths to lead the eye towards the ground. If you want a different view, Norris Reserve gives a distant skyline panorama with the ground as one part of the frame. On match days the park is used for parking and gets very crowded, so a quiet day is much easier for photos. If you plan to go inside the stadium, check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The ground stands in Yarra Park in the suburb of East Melbourne, Victoria.
text.directions_text: The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the stands, floodlights and trees together. Then try the default lens (1x) for a more natural view. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the floodlights and roofline above the treetops.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Yarra Park (west of the ground, near Jolimont station, looking back at the stadium). The MCG's floodlights and stands rising above the trees of the park, with the ground seen across open lawn and paths.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the stadium along the upper third, with lawn or a path in the lower part of the frame. Keep the horizon level, because the large stands make any tilt obvious. Let the trees frame the edges, and wait for people to walk out of your shot. For a wider view with the ground as only one part of the scene, Norris Reserve gives a distant city skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the floodlights or the stand roofs to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the stadium does not wash out. Use the telephoto for detail and the ultra-wide for scale.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a day with no match, as the park is busy with parking and crowds on match days. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light.

text.access_note: Check the official MCG site for access and event information before you go.

name: Eureka Tower
label: Eureka Tower
camera_source: No separate stand-here point: photographed at the spot itself (indoors, from its top, or right in front of it); drawn as the split pin.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13307317: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Eureka Tower' (156 m across).
notes: Skyscraper with the Skydeck 88 observation deck over the city.

text.description:
Eureka Tower is a 297.3 m glass skyscraper in the Southbank part of Melbourne, finished in 2006 and officially opened on 11 October 2006. Its looks tell a story. The design draws on the Eureka Stockade, the 1854 rebellion during the Victorian gold rush. The gold crown stands for the gold rush, the red stripe for the blood spilt, and the blue glass and white lines for the colours of the stockade flag. That makes it easy to photograph, because the colours and bands read clearly even on a small phone screen.

At the base there is an art installation of gold bees in and around a white box, like a man-made beehive. If you can find it, it is a good foreground detail to include when you point your phone upwards. The tower's top floors hold the Melbourne Skydeck on level 88, which is the highest public viewing floor in a building in the Southern Hemisphere. An entry fee applies there, so if you want pictures from inside, check the official site before you go.

For the best result, think about shape rather than detail. The tower is very tall and narrow, so a photo from close by needs the camera tilted up, which can make the sides lean inwards. Keep the phone as upright as you can and use the gridlines to line up the edges. A few steps back, or a slightly different angle, will often help more than zooming.
text.geographic_location: Eureka Tower is in the Southbank precinct of Melbourne, Victoria.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so use the map to reach Southbank, the area where the tower stands. Look for the 297.3 m tower with its gold crown. Once you are near the building, follow the map towards the phone icon on the map at the centre of the tower's outline, then move to a safe spot outside the building and step back to fit the tower in. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for a close-up shot of the whole tower. Use the default lens (1x) for the base, the bees and the lower levels. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) from further back for the gold crown and the red stripe.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. This is a close-up spot, not a distant view. Move to a safe spot outside near the building and step back as far as you can to fit more of the tower in, tilting the phone upwards as needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the tower's vertical edges up with them. Hold the phone as upright as you can, because tilting it steeply makes the tower lean. Include the gold bees at the base as foreground if you can find the bee installation, and let the tower lead the eye up to the gold crown. Portrait orientation suits the tower's height.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the glass to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not wash out the blue glass and the gold top. If your phone has a Live Photo or motion option, switch it off for this shot and keep the phone still instead.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is usually kinder to the glass than harsh midday light, and a clear day shows the blue cladding and gold top best. Check the sun's direction on the day, as it decides which face of the tower is lit.

text.access_note: The Melbourne Skydeck on level 88 has an entry fee, so check the official site before you go.

name: National Gallery of Victoria
label: NGV International
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Birrarung Marr' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Birrarung Marr' (way/46330961): middle (594 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/23764181: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'National Gallery of Victoria' (264 m across).
notes: Famous water wall at the entrance of the art gallery.

text.description: The National Gallery of Victoria, known as the NGV, was founded in 1861 and is Australia's oldest and most visited art museum. The building on this map is NGV International at 180 St Kilda Road, designed by Sir Roy Grounds and opened in 1968. It is clad in bluestone, is on the Victorian Heritage Register, and was redeveloped by Mario Bellini before reopening in 2003. This is a context shot rather than a close-up. The gallery sits among the southern-bank buildings, their reflections run along the water, and some of the nearby towers fill out the frame. Because the gallery is some way off, think of it as one part of a wider riverside scene. Use the telephoto lens if you want it larger in the picture. For a closer, more detailed picture, the water-wall entrance on St Kilda Road is the other classic view, with the bluestone building rising behind it. The water wall is a well-known feature of the building and was kept, in a new position slightly forward of the original, when the gallery was redeveloped. Inside, the Leonard French stained-glass ceiling casts coloured light on the floor below, but photography rules can differ between galleries, so check signage.
text.geographic_location: NGV International stands on St Kilda Road in the Melbourne Arts Precinct of Southbank, just south of the Yarra River.
text.directions_text: From there the gallery lies about 650 m to the south-west across the river. To reach the gallery itself at 180 St Kilda Road, head south-west across the river. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to capture the river, the reflections and the towers together. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the gallery closer. Use ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of foreground, such as the riverbank, and accept that the gallery will look small.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Birrarung Marr (northern riverbank of the Yarra, facing south). The gallery across the river, with its buildings reflected along the Yarra and nearby towers in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the water along the lower third, so the reflections take up part of the picture. Keep the horizon level and the building edges straight. Let the gallery sit off-centre among the other riverside buildings. For a closer alternative, go to the water-wall entrance on St Kilda Road and photograph the wall with the bluestone building behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the buildings to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky does not wash out and the reflections stay rich. If you shoot on the telephoto lens, hold the phone steady with both hands and elbows tucked in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a calm, bright day, since still water gives the clearest reflections. Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the buildings.

text.access_note: Birrarung Marr is an open public park, but check the official site before you go for current closures or works, and for the gallery's photography rules, as ticketed exhibitions may restrict photography.
claims_not_in_sources: Calm water gives clearer reflections than choppy water.
Morning or late afternoon light is usually softer than midday light.

name: Queen Victoria Market
label: Queen Victoria Market
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Elizabeth Street' (1 web pages); placed at the stretch of Elizabeth Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/25467961: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Queen Victoria Market' (290 m across).
notes: Large open-air market dating from 1878.

text.description: Queen Victoria Market, known locally as the Vic Market, is a big, busy, working market in the middle of Melbourne. It covers more than seven hectares and is the largest open air market in the Southern Hemisphere. For a phone photo, the best whole-building view is from Elizabeth Street, where the old market frontage lines up along the pavement. The shops along this side date from 1880. The well-known Meat and Fish Hall facade was added in 1884 and is still largely intact, which gives you a strong heritage subject with the street framing it. The market officially opened in March 1878, and it is on both the Victorian Heritage Register and the National Heritage List. It was built over the site of Melbourne's first British burial ground, the Old Melbourne Cemetery, which is a good story to tell your travel companions while you shoot. Take one wide, straight-on shot of the facade first, then move closer for details such as signs, rooflines and stall awnings. Look at the edges of the frame: poles, parked vehicles and passers-by are easy to catch by accident, so take a few frames and keep the best. If you want a second angle, String Bean Alley has handmade stalls that suit close detail shots. The corner of Therry Street and Queen Street is good for the busy market-edge crowd. Check opening days before you go, as the market is not open every day.
text.geographic_location: In Melbourne's central business district, on the Elizabeth Street side of the market block that is bounded by Victoria, Peel, Franklin and Elizabeth streets. The Meat and Fish Hall stands on the corner of Elizabeth and Victoria streets.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so head for Queen Victoria Market in Melbourne's city centre by taxi or hired scooter and ask to be dropped on Elizabeth Street. Walk along the pavement until the whole facade fits in your screen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if the pavement is narrow and you want the whole facade in one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look with less edge stretching. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as signs and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Elizabeth Street (facade of the market along Elizabeth Street). The market's historic 1884 facade, framed by the street, as a whole-building shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line the building up with the horizontal lines so the roofline looks straight. Hold the phone level, as tilting it up makes the building lean. Keep a little street in the foreground to show scale. For a different view, try String Bean Alley for stall details, or the corner of Therry Street and Queen Street for the crowd at the market's edge.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the facade to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is bright, so the brickwork and signs keep their colour. Use a Live Photo if people or traffic are moving, so you can pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, soon after the market opens, is often said to have the best light. Check which days the market is open before you go.

text.access_note: The facade can be photographed from the public street, but trading days and times vary, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.

name: Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria
label: Royal Botanic Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Picnic Point' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Picnic Point' (way/1011910840): middle (67 m across).
pin_note: Position set at the correction gate (pin check 2026-11-17: moved onto the OSM object with the sight's Wikidata ID).
notes: Large landscaped gardens with lake and city skyline views.

text.description: The Royal Botanic Gardens Victoria's Melbourne Gardens cover 38 hectares on the south side of the Yarra River. They were founded in 1846 and now hold almost 50,000 plants from about 8,500 species. The site has been on the Victorian Heritage Register since 1982. This spot is about the lake rather than any single bed or building. The Ornamental Lake was shaped around the turn of the 20th century from the old wetland. Its still water gives you a clean, open foreground, with the gardens' trees and lakeside buildings along the far bank. From Picnic Point you look across the water towards The Terrace cafe, so the picture has a clear sequence: water, tree line, then buildings. Phones cope well with this kind of scene because there is nothing close to the lens to confuse the focus. Keep the shot simple. Put the waterline on a gridline, leave some room for the sky, and wait for a quiet moment with no one walking into the frame. If you want a different view, the Ornamental Lake can also be framed as a reflective foreground with the city skyline rising beyond the trees. Guilfoyle's Volcano is another option, with cacti in the foreground and views over the city. Check the official site before you go, because some features and lookouts are closed from time to time.
text.geographic_location: The Melbourne Gardens lie on the south side of the Yarra River in the City of Melbourne, next to Government House, Melbourne Observatory and the Kings Domain. Picnic Point is on the lakeside of the Ornamental Lake; confirm the exact position on the map.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops or stations are listed for this spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full sweep of lake, trees and buildings. Try 2x to pick out The Terrace across the water and cut out empty foreground. The ultra-wide (0.5x) works for a big sky, but it makes the far bank look small and distant.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Picnic Point (lakeside, looking across Ornamental Lake toward The Terrace cafe). Ornamental Lake in the foreground with the gardens' lakeside trees and buildings beyond the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the far bank on the upper third line so the water fills the lower part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the waterline doesn't slope. If you have time, the Ornamental Lake also works as a reflective foreground with the city skyline above the trees, and Guilfoyle's Volcano gives a different view of the city from inside the gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the far bank to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the water doesn't wash out. A Live Photo can help you pick the frame with the cleanest ripples or no passers-by.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Pick a calm day for the clearest reflections. Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the water.

text.access_note: The gardens are a public botanic garden, but individual areas and lookouts can be closed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Flinders Street railway station
label: Flinders Street Statio
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Federation Square' (2 web pages); placed at crossing of Flinders Street and Swanston Street (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/4936370201: the OpenStreetMap point 'Flinders Street'.
notes: Iconic yellow Edwardian station facade opposite Federation Square.

text.description:
Flinders Street station is the building most people picture when they think of central Melbourne. The current station was completed in 1909, and its Edwardian frontage has a prominent dome, an arched main entrance, a tower and a row of clocks above the doors. Those clocks give Melburnians their meeting line, "I'll meet you under the clocks", and the wide steps below them are another favourite spot to wait. The station site is older than the building: a railway station opened here in 1854, and it is described as the oldest in Australia, though not the present building. The building has been on the Victorian Heritage Register since 1982, and it is still the busiest station in Victoria, so there is always something happening in front of it.

It photographs well because the facade is big, detailed and easy to read, and trams and people cross in front of it all day. That gives your picture a sense of scale and movement. From the Federation Square side you can fit the dome and the Swanston Street front into one shot, with trams passing in the foreground. If you want the clocks and the arched entrance as the main subject, St Paul's Cathedral gives the most direct view. Princes Bridge offers a third angle, with trams running towards the intersection and the station on one side. Stay on the footpaths at all times and keep clear of tram tracks and crossings. Scaffolding sometimes covers part of the front, so check before making a special trip.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Melbourne, on the corner of Flinders and Swanston streets, directly across the intersection from Federation Square and close to St Paul's Cathedral. The station backs onto the Yarra River.
text.directions_text: Head for Federation Square in the middle of Melbourne. Cross at the pedestrian lights and keep to the footpaths. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to get the dome and the Swanston Street side in one frame. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the building will not fit, or to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the clocks and the arched entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at the corner of Flinders Street and Swanston Street (south-east corner of the intersection, at the edge of Federation Square, looking west across Swanston Street). The dome and the Swanston Street side of the station fill the frame, with trams crossing in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the dome near an upper third line, keeping the vertical lines straight. Wait for a tram to cross the lower part of the frame so it adds movement without hiding the building. For a closer view of the row of clocks, the arched entrance and the dome stacked above it, try St Paul's Cathedral side instead, and Princes Bridge gives trams leading towards the intersection.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the facade to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the sky and the stonework keep their detail. Take a Live Photo or a short burst when trams pass, then pick the best frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, when the sun lights this side of the building. For an evening shot, try blue hour once the lights come on, and switch on night mode if your phone does not do it automatically.

text.access_note: The outside is on public footpaths and open to view; inside the station, personal photography is allowed without flash or tripods, but check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Trams cross in front of the station throughout the day, so there is usually one to wait for.
Ultra-wide (0.5x) may be needed if the whole building will not fit from the Federation Square corner.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in the sky and the stonework.

name: Melbourne Museum
label: Melbourne Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Carlton Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Carlton Gardens' (relation/6614802): edge nearest the subject (867 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4817074: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Melbourne Museum' (284 m across).
notes: Large museum next to Carlton Gardens.

text.description:
Melbourne Museum is a natural and cultural history museum set inside Carlton Gardens, right beside the Royal Exhibition Building. It opened in October 2000 and was designed by Denton Corker Marshall. For a phone photographer the appeal is the building's shape. Long, sloping blade-like canopies rise from the central entrance, and the angular forms contrast nicely with the green lawns and the older Victorian-era buildings around them. The museum lines up with the Royal Exhibition Building across an events plaza, so the two make a good old-meets-new pairing. Inside, the Forest Gallery is a living piece of Victorian forest, which gives you a good reason to go in once you have your outside shots.

From there the museum is to the south, so face that way and use the open lawns as your foreground. Keep the angled roof lines as the main subject and let the grass and trees fill the lower part of the frame. If you have time, try two other views: the western edge of the gardens, where the colourful tilted cube of the Children's Museum sits at one side, and Nicholson Street, where the glassy main entrance faces you as you approach. The museum won Best Tourist Attraction at the Australian Tourism Awards in 2011, so expect other visitors to be around.
text.geographic_location: Melbourne Museum stands in Carlton Gardens, in the suburb of Carlton. It is next to the Royal Exhibition Building.
text.directions_text: No public transport stops are listed for this spot, so check a journey planner and walk to Carlton Gardens. Aim for the Royal Exhibition Building, as the museum is right next to it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the lawn to get the whole building with some grass in front. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you stand close and want the sweep of the canopies. Try 2x if you want to pick out the angular roof lines from further back.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Carlton Gardens (south side of the gardens). The museum's neo-constructivist southern elevation seen across the lawns from the gardens' southern side. The museum's angular forms should rise across the lawns in front of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the building's vertical edges with them, so the walls don't lean. Keep the sloping roof lines as the main subject and let the lawn fill the bottom of the frame. For a second shot, walk to the western edge of the gardens to get the colourful tilted cube of the Children's Museum at one side, or go to Nicholson Street for the glass entrance.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the walls keep their detail. Take a few frames in case people walk through.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No fixed best time. Low, softer sun usually flatters angular buildings, so early morning or late afternoon on a clear day is worth trying.

text.access_note: Carlton Gardens is a public park, but entry to the museum itself may be ticketed, so check the official site before you go.

name: Federation Square
label: Federation Square
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Federation Square' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Federation Square' (way/1098427843): middle (358 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Federation Square'.
notes: Angular, colourful civic square beside the Yarra.

text.description:
Federation Square, known locally as Fed Square, is a public square and cultural centre on the edge of Melbourne's central business district. It sits at the corner of Flinders and Swanston Streets, directly across the road from Flinders Street station. It covers about 3.2 hectares and is built over busy railway lines. Around the paved square you'll find the Ian Potter Centre, the Australian Centre for the Moving Image (ACMI), the Koorie Heritage Trust, and a number of cafes and bars.

It photographs well because of its geometry. The design uses gently angled, 'cranked' shapes, with tall shards as vertical accents, and the facades are made of several different materials. The result is a pattern of sharp edges and panels that look good with sky behind them. The square opened on 26 October 2002. It cost about $467 million, over four times the first estimate.

Switch to the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) so the full set of angles and the sky fit in the frame. Afternoon is the time to aim for, when the panels catch direct light and the shadows deepen. The central plaza can be busy with crowds and events, so expect people in your shot and be ready to wait for a gap or to use them for scale. Guides recommend the northwest corner of the square as a viewpoint; that is a separate suggestion, so check it on the day. If you want a second view, Princes Bridge and Evan Walker Bridge both show the square's edge with Flinders Street station and the Yarra River.
text.geographic_location: Federation Square is on the edge of Melbourne's central business district, at the corner of Flinders and Swanston Streets. It stands opposite Flinders Street station, with the Yarra River just to the south.
text.directions_text: Aim for the corner of Flinders and Swanston Streets, directly across the road from Flinders Street station, on the edge of the central business district. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the ultra-wide lens (0.5x) for the main shot, so the whole angular facade and plenty of sky fit in. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view of one section. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out repeating panels and sharp edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Federation Square (northwest corner of the square, looking southeast toward the main facade). The angular, multi-material main facade of Federation Square, with sky included at a wide-angle focal length. From here you look towards the main facade, with its angular, multi-material surfaces and the sky above. name: Shrine of Remembrance
label: Shrine of Remembrance
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shrine of Remembrance' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24590190: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Shrine of Remembrance' (55 m across).
notes: War memorial with city views from its upper balcony.

text.description:
The Shrine of Remembrance stands in Kings Domain on St Kilda Road. It was built to honour Victorians who served in World War I, and today it is a memorial to all Australians who have served in any war. It is one of the largest war memorials in Australia. Its stepped, classical shape was designed by two veteran architects, Phillip Hudson and James Wardrop, and draws on the Parthenon and the ancient tomb at Halicarnassus. The granite was quarried at Tynong, and the Shrine was dedicated on 11 November 1934.

It photographs well because the strong, symmetrical stonework sits on a rise above open parkland. The most rewarding view is from the upper Balcony around the rooftop terrace, where you look out over the city skyline rising from the surrounding gardens. The forecourt steps are the alternative: from there the skyline sits beyond the parkland, with the Shrine's stepped approach at your back. The steps are outdoors and can be reached at any time, while the balcony is reached through the building.

Photography is allowed inside the building but not in the galleries. Please keep clear of any wreath-laying or ceremony and do not photograph it. Take a few frames from the steps and a few from the balcony, as they give very different pictures.
text.geographic_location: The Shrine is in Kings Domain on the east side of St Kilda Road, south of Melbourne's city centre.
text.directions_text: From the city centre, head south along St Kilda Road until you reach Kings Domain, where the Shrine stands on the rise on the eastern side. Once there, enter the building if you want the upper balcony, or climb the forecourt steps for the outdoor view. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the skyline from the balcony. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in a wider sweep of the rooftop terrace and gardens. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out individual towers in the city skyline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you get a panoramic view of the city skyline rising out of the surrounding gardens. For a second view, stand on the forecourt steps and shoot towards the city skyline across the parkland, with the stepped approach at your back.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and set the horizon on the lower or upper third line. Include some of the gardens in the foreground so the skyline has depth. Rotate through the terrace for a few different angles, or try a panorama. Keep the phone level, as tilting it will lean the towers.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the skyline to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the city keeps its detail. Hold your phone steady, away from the railing, and clean the lens first.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visiting hours decide when you can reach the balcony, so check the official site before you go. Late afternoon or early morning light tends to be softer for the skyline. The forecourt steps are open at any time.

text.access_note: The forecourt steps are outdoors, but the upper balcony is reached through the building and is open only during visiting hours, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Late afternoon or early morning light tends to be softer for skyline photos.

notes: Cobbled laneway famous for ever-changing street art.

text.description:
Hosier Lane is a narrow street in Melbourne whose walls are covered in street art. It photographs well because the painted walls rise on both sides and seem to close in towards the far end, so the lane works like a colourful tunnel. The lane also curves slightly, which leads the eye along it towards the south end.

The classic picture is taken from the Flinders Street (north) entrance, looking up the lane. From there you see its full length, with the art on both walls converging in the distance. If you walk in, the junction of the two lanes offers a dense cluster of layered murals, doors and walls, which suits closer, more detailed shots. Rutledge Lane, the horseshoe-shaped side lane, is a good alternative: it gives a longer view down a passage with layered graffiti and paste-ups.

The murals are repainted often, so what you see may not match the pictures you have seen online. One photographer found the entrance much brighter than the back of the lane, so the contrast may be strong; check how your phone handles it before you take the shot. Come early in the morning if you can, before the crowds arrive. The lane is narrow, so keep to the side when you stop to shoot and let people pass.
text.geographic_location: Hosier Lane is in Melbourne, running south from Flinders Street.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot. Head for Flinders Street in Melbourne and look for the lane entrance on Flinders Street. The phone icon on the map marks where to start. Once you are in the lane, the junction of the two lanes is further along the lane. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in both painted walls and the whole length of the lane. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out a single mural or detail.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you see the full length of the lane, with the painted walls on both sides converging towards the far end.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Centre the lane so the walls lead into the distance, and turn on gridlines to keep the verticals straight. Wait for a gap in the people if you want a clear tunnel effect, or include them to show the scale. For an alternative, walk to the junction for layered murals and doors, or look down Rutledge Lane for a longer view.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: One photographer found the entrance much brighter than the back of the lane, so the contrast may be strong. Tap on the darker part of the lane to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky or entrance looks washed out. Check the result and retake if needed.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, before the crowds arrive.

text.access_note: Hosier Lane is a public lane open to walk through, but whether one-way vehicles use it can vary, so check on the day and stay alert; check the official site before you go for any closures.

text.description: State Library Victoria fills a whole block of central Melbourne and is a good place to practise photographing architecture on a phone. It was established in 1854 as the Melbourne Public Library (first stage opened in 1856), which makes it Australia's oldest public library and one of the first free libraries in the world. The Swanston Street front is the classic view, with its classical portico (added in 1870), and the grand stone walls give you strong lines to work with. Inside, the famous Domed Reading Room opened in 1913. Its skylights were hidden behind copper sheathing from 1959 and were revealed again when it reopened as the La Trobe Reading Room in 2003. The collection runs to over five million items, including Ned Kelly's armour and the original Jerilderie Letter. For a phone, the building suits wide shots that show off the columns and steps, and tighter shots of details such as stonework and rooflines. Stand back far enough to fit the portico in, and keep the gridlines on so the columns stay upright. If you go inside, the reading rooms are very photogenic, but take care to be quiet and considerate around people who are studying. Rules on photography indoors can change, so it is worth checking before you raise your phone.
text.geographic_location: In the central business district of Melbourne, on Swanston Street. The library covers the block also bounded by La Trobe, Russell and Little Lonsdale streets.
text.directions_text: The library is in the Melbourne central business district, on Swanston Street, with its front facing the street. The spot data gives no nearby stations or tram stops, so follow the map to the phone icon on the map. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the full width of the building and the portico, then switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural look. Use the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for carvings, columns and rooflines.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Move back along the street to fit the whole building in.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the columns with the vertical lines so the building does not lean. Keep the portico in the centre and let the steps lead the eye in. If you go inside, use portrait orientation for the tall reading-room spaces, and shoot upwards to include the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building's stonework to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the facade keeps its detail. Indoors, hold the phone steady against a rail or your body, and let night mode take over if the room is dim.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the stonework. Early on a weekday is often calmer for exterior shots.

name: Royal Exhibition Building

camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Nicholson Street' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Nicholson Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).

notes: UNESCO-listed 1880 dome in Carlton Gardens.

text.description:
The Royal Exhibition Building is the big, cream-coloured exhibition hall in Carlton Gardens, with a tall dome rising above long, symmetrical wings. It was built in 1879-1880 to host the Melbourne International Exhibition, and in 2004 it became the first building in Australia to receive UNESCO World Heritage status. The dome was modelled on Florence Cathedral and rises about 68 metres. The hall is about 150 metres long, which is why it can be hard to fit in from close by.

It photographs well because the setting does half the work. From the street you get the full south facade and dome across the ornamental pond, with the water, lawns and trees leading the eye towards the building. A heritage study of old postcards found this stretch of Nicholson Street was the standard view, and it is still the main near view today.

If you want something closer, walk in towards the entrance steps and the fountain, with the dome behind. For a quieter, more natural frame, go into Carlton Gardens and shoot the building's bulk through the planting. Exhibitions can clutter the background, so look at the scene before you pick your angle.
text.geographic_location: The building stands in Carlton Gardens, on the north-eastern edge of Melbourne's central business district, next to Melbourne Museum. Its address is 9 Nicholson Street.
text.directions_text: From the north-eastern edge of the city centre, head for Nicholson Street on the east side of Carlton Gardens. The nearest stations and tram stops could not be confirmed, so check a map app for the best way to get there. From there the building is to the west, about 3 minutes on foot if you want to walk in for a closer view. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) from the street so the pond, the facade and the dome all sit in one frame. Switch to the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the dome. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you move close to the steps and want the whole front in view.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Nicholson Street (stretch between Gertrude Street and Victoria Street, opposite the south facade). The full southern facade and dome of the building framed across the ornamental pond, the classic postcard composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the central vertical line, with the pond in the lower part of the frame so its reflection and the lawns lead up to the building. Keep the phone level so the facade does not lean. For a different shot, go to the entrance steps for a close frontal view with the fountain in the foreground, or into Carlton Gardens for a ground-level view of the building's height framed by the planting.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the facade keeps its detail. Take a few shots at 1x and at a longer zoom so you can choose later.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or early morning gives the best light. Around the fountain, midday summer sun can be harsh.

text.access_note: Carlton Gardens is a public park with no entry charge, but access to the front steps can be restricted during exhibitions and the Melbourne flower show, so check the official site before you go.

name: Old Melbourne Gaol
label: Old Melbourne Gaol
camera_source: Commons cluster (2 photos), weak.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/26564392: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Old Melbourne Gaol' (71 m across).
notes: Historic bluestone jail where Ned Kelly was hanged.

text.description:
The Old Melbourne Gaol is a former prison that is now a museum, and its dark bluestone walls make it one of the most characterful old buildings in the city. It stands on Russell Street beside the old City Police Watch House and City Courts, and opposite the Russell Street Police Headquarters, so the whole street has a sombre, historic feel. Building began in 1839. It worked as a prison from 1845 until 1924, and 133 people were hanged there, among them the bushranger Ned Kelly in November 1880. By 1864 the perimeter wall and the gaol were complete, and the site filled an entire city block. Today the museum shows the stories of prisoners and staff, including death masks of executed men.

For photographs, the strength of the place is its texture: heavy stone, blank walls and small, severe openings. They look dramatic even in plain light. That is far enough to take in a good length of the frontage and the street in front of it. Hold the phone level, use the gridlines to keep the walls straight, and include a little pavement or sky so the stone feels tall and solid. If you go inside, photography rules may differ, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: In central Melbourne, on Russell Street near the corner with La Trobe Street. It sits next to the old City Police Watch House and City Courts buildings.
text.directions_text: No tram or railway stops are listed for this spot. Head for Russell Street in central Melbourne and ask for the Old Melbourne Gaol. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full frontage. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the bluestone texture and small details. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you get close to the walls and want to show their height.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (Russell Street front facade, at the main entrance). The bluestone front of the gaol with its heavy iron gates, framed by the Russell Street footpath.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the top of the wall with a horizontal line so the building does not lean. Keep a strip of pavement at the bottom and some sky at the top to give a sense of scale. Then zoom in for a tighter shot of stonework and windows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the dark bluestone keeps its detail and the sky does not turn white.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning or a bright, slightly cloudy day should suit this view, because the stone shows its texture without harsh glare.

text.access_note: The gaol is a museum, so entry is likely to be ticketed; check the official site before you go.

name: Fitzroy Gardens
label: Fitzroy Gardens
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fitzroy Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fitzroy Gardens' (way/4817020): edge nearest the subject (830 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/4817020: large area 'Fitzroy Gardens' (833 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Tree-lined gardens with Cooks' Cottage and the conservatory.

text.description:
Fitzroy Gardens is a large Victorian-era park on the south-eastern edge of Melbourne's city centre, and its best-known picture is the long avenue of elm trees. Stand at one end and the path runs away from you under a leafy roof, which gives a simple, strong photo: trees on both sides, a path leading the eye, and the canopy filling the top of the frame. In autumn, from March to May, the elms turn gold and the scene is at its best.

The gardens cover about 26 hectares and were set aside as public gardens in 1848. The elms were planted along the paths, and together the avenues happen to form a pattern like the Union Jack. They were laid out as shady walking routes, so the avenue was made to be walked along and looked down. The park also holds Cooks' Cottage, a conservatory, a lake and a model Tudor village, so there is plenty to photograph on the same visit.

For the avenue shot, keep the path central and the trees on either side level, and crouch a little so the path leads further into the picture. Early morning light is softer under the trees. If you have time, Cook's Cottage with its garden and the Boy on the Turtle pond with its wooden bridge make good second stops. Check conditions before you go, as paths or areas can close for seasonal work.
text.geographic_location: Fitzroy Gardens is in East Melbourne, just south-east of the city centre. It sits between Clarendon Street, Albert Street, Lansdowne Street and Wellington Parade, with Treasury Gardens across the road to the west.
text.directions_text: There is no tram or railway stop right at this spot, so from the city centre head south-east towards East Melbourne on foot or by taxi and aim for the gardens. Follow the path east towards the elm avenue and use the map to find the exact spot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the whole avenue and canopy fit. If your phone has a 2x telephoto, try it too: it squeezes the trees together and makes the avenue look longer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a more dramatic, sweeping view, and keep the phone level so the trees don't lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Fitzroy Gardens (one end of the central elm avenue, looking down the path). The long tree-lined elm avenue receding into the distance, with the canopy filling the upper frame and the path leading the eye. Walk east to one end of the central elm avenue and look down the path from there. Stand in the middle of the path so both sides match.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the path on the centre line, with the trees balanced either side. Hold the phone low, around knee height, for a stronger sense of depth. If you have time, Cook's Cottage and the Boy on the Turtle pond are two other good photo stops in the gardens.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the path in the middle distance to set focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright gaps in the canopy do not turn white. Take a few shots in a row, as people often walk through the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Autumn (March to May) for the golden elm leaves, and early morning for softer light and gentler shadows under the canopy.

text.access_note: The gardens are a public park run by the City of Melbourne. Check the City of Melbourne site for current access details before you go.

name: Arts Centre Melbourne
label: Arts Centre Spire
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Arts Centre Melbourne' (3 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).

text.description: Arts Centre Melbourne is the city's performing arts complex, and from the rear of the building the thing to photograph is the latticework spire. It stands above the Theatres Building, with Hamer Hall alongside, in the Melbourne Arts Precinct at Southbank. Standing underneath, you can look straight up through the criss-cross of the spire and see it against the sky and the surrounding buildings. That makes a bold, graphic picture even if the buildings themselves are not especially pretty. The architect Sir Roy Grounds planned the complex, and the masterplan was approved in 1960. Hamer Hall opened in 1982 and the Theatres Building in 1984. The spire was topped off with its lightning conductor rod in 1981, and the original idea was a spire 115 m tall. Much of the centre is built underground. For a phone, make the spire your subject and use the sky as a clean background. Try one wide shot that shows how the spire rises from the buildings, then a tighter one on the lattice pattern. If you want a view with the river, Princes Bridge shows the spire rising above the circular Theatres Building with the Yarra in front, and River Terrace shows Hamer Hall and the spire across the river (check River Terrace on a map first). Check the official site if you are planning to go inside, as performances and events may affect access.
text.geographic_location: Arts Centre Melbourne is in Southbank, just south of the Yarra River, beside St Kilda Road in the Melbourne Arts Precinct.
text.directions_text: From the centre of Melbourne, head south across the Yarra River towards Southbank and St Kilda Road, where the spire is easy to spot. Once you arrive, go round to the rear of the complex, between Hamer Hall and the Theatres Building, and stand under the spire. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole spire and the buildings around it into one upward shot. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a calmer, less stretched view, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the lattice pattern.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. The Theatres Building and its spire are directly at this point, so the photo is a close-up looking up from ground level.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the spire up with a vertical line so it does not lean. Keep the sky clear around the tip for a clean, graphic shot, or let a corner of a building frame one side. For a different view with the water, try Princes Bridge, or River Terrace for Hamer Hall and the spire across the Yarra.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the spire to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. After dark, use night mode and rest your arms against a wall or railing to keep the phone still.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk and after dark, when the spire is lit up, is especially striking. In daylight, a clear sky gives the cleanest background.

text.access_note: Photography is generally allowed outside and in the foyer of Hamer Hall, but not during performances; check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Southbank lies south of the Yarra River and the city centre.

name: Princes Bridge
label: Princes Bridge
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Southbank Promenade' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Southbank Promenade nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/70955791: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Princes Bridge' (132 m across).
notes: Classic view of the skyline and Yarra River.

text.description: Princes Bridge is a gateway into Melbourne's city centre from the south, connecting the city centre and Southbank. It carries Swanston Street over the Yarra River and on to St Kilda Road, and it has trams, cyclists and walkers crossing all day. It photographs well because you can stand on the south bank and fit the whole bridge in the foreground, with the city towers rising behind it. On calm mornings and evenings the water can act as a mirror. The bridge you see today opened on 4 October 1888, and it was added to the Victorian Heritage Register in 1982. It stands on the site of one of the city's oldest river crossings, and parts of the stone from the earlier 1850 bridge were reused in it. Its bluestone piers and cast-iron detail give the picture a solid, old-fashioned feel against the glass towers. Use the wide view so the arches, the river and the skyline all fit in one frame. If you have time, a second view is worth a look from outside Arts Centre Melbourne, which is on the Southbank side, a short walk along St Kilda Road from the bridge. It puts the bridge in front of the Yarra and the skyline from a different angle. The bridge is busy, so keep to the pavement and out of the tram tracks while you shoot.
text.geographic_location: Princes Bridge crosses the Yarra River in the centre of Melbourne. It links Swanston Street on the north bank with St Kilda Road in Southbank, near the Arts Precinct and Federation Square.
text.directions_text: Start from the centre of Melbourne at the Swanston Street end of the bridge, cross the river on foot, and take the riverside path on the Southbank side. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole bridge, the river and the skyline into one frame. The default lens (1x) is a good second shot and gives a calmer, less stretched look. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it to pick out the towers behind the bridge.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Southbank Promenade (south bank of the Yarra, riverbank near Hamer Hall, a little upstream of the bridge). The bridge in the foreground with the CBD towers rising behind it, best captured with a wide lens. The bridge sits in front of you to the north, with the city towers rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and place the bridge along the lower third, so the towers fill the upper part and the water fills the foreground. Keep the phone level so the bridge rail does not slope. For a different view, the free ground-level spot outside Arts Centre Melbourne, on the Southbank side, shows the bridge with the river and skyline behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the bridge to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky keeps its colour and the lights stay sharp. At dusk, use night mode and brace your elbows against your body or a railing to keep the phone still. A Live Photo can catch trams and walkers crossing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Blue hour or sunrise. Calm mornings and evenings give the best reflections in the river.

text.access_note: The bridge and the riverside promenade are open public spaces with no ticket needed, but check the official site before you go in case of works or event closures.
claims_not_in_sources: The viewpoint on the south bank looks north towards the bridge and the city skyline.
Calm water at dusk or dawn can give reflections of the bridge and lights.
Trams and walkers crossing the bridge can add movement to a Live Photo.
Federation Square is close to the north end of the bridge.

name: Block Arcade
label: Block Arcade
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Collins Street' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Collins Street nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/46751453: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Block Arcade' (102 m across).
notes: Ornate 1892 arcade with mosaic floors and glass canopy.

text.description:
Block Arcade is a Victorian shopping arcade in the middle of Melbourne, built between 1891 and 1893 and designed by the architects Twentyman & Askew. The Collins Street end opened first, and the whole arcade had its grand opening on 7 October 1893. The name comes from "doing the block", the fashionable habit of strolling along this stretch of Collins Street to see and be seen.

This spot is about the street-level view. From the footpath in front of the Collins Street entrance you can see the six-storey frontage and the doorway that leads into the arcade, with the street and passing traffic beside it. It is the classic way to photograph the arcade, and an old photo of the same spot shows the view has barely changed. The frontage is also described as one of Australia's best surviving examples of Victorian Mannerist architecture.

Once you have the outside shot, go in. The arcade is L-shaped, with an octagonal rotunda at the corner, a mosaic tiled floor, a glass canopy on cast and wrought iron, and tall timber shop fronts. The mosaic floor radiating from the rotunda, with the domed glass ceiling and wrought-iron balconies above, makes a good second picture. The quieter Elizabeth Street entrance gives a view down the covered walkway towards the dome, but check that entrance is open when you arrive. Expect shoppers, especially around midday, so be patient and shoot between groups.
text.geographic_location: Block Arcade is in Melbourne's central business district, on the north side of Collins Street between Swanston and Elizabeth streets. It links Collins Street, Elizabeth Street and, via Block Place, Little Collins Street opposite the Royal Arcade.
text.directions_text: Head for Collins Street in the central business district, between Swanston Street and Elizabeth Street. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the frontage and doorway. If the footpath is too narrow to fit the six storeys in, switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x). Use the telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the ornate details higher up.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Collins Street (on the footpath in front of the Collins Street entrance, facing the arcade's ornate frontage). The six-storey Victorian Collins Street facade and entrance doorway framing the arcade, with the street and passing traffic beside it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the doorway in the centre and keep your phone upright so the vertical lines stay straight. Switch on gridlines to help. If the street is busy, wait for a gap in the crowd. For a second picture, go inside and shoot the mosaic floor and domed ceiling from the rotunda, or use the Elizabeth Street entrance for the view down the covered walkway.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the doorway to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the street is bright and the entrance looks too dark. Inside, tap on the floor or dome and hold the phone steady, as the light is softer. Night mode may kick in automatically, so brace your elbows against your body.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: No photo-specific times are known. The arcade can be crowded and busy with shoppers around midday, so an earlier or quieter part of the day should give you a clearer view.

text.access_note: The street view is from a public footpath, but the arcade is an indoor shopping space, so check the official site before you go for opening times and any photography rules.
claims_not_in_sources: An earlier or quieter part of the day should be less crowded than midday.
The footpath in front of the entrance may be narrow enough that the ultra-wide lens helps fit in the whole frontage.
Night mode may switch on automatically in the dimmer interior.

name: Parliament House, Melbourne
label: Parliament House
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Parliament Gardens' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Parliament Gardens' (way/27783990): middle (175 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/24530652: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Parliament House' (146 m across).
notes: Neoclassical building at the top of Bourke Street.

text.description: Parliament House is where the Parliament of Victoria meets, and its grand colonnaded front looks straight down Bourke Street from the top of the hill. That is what makes it such a strong subject. The columns give you bold lines and repeating shapes, and the long street below gives you depth. Building began in 1855, and the first session in the new chambers opened on 25 November 1856. The building has never been finished, and the dome that was planned for it is one of Melbourne's best-known unbuilt features. From 1901 to 1927 it also housed the national Parliament, while Melbourne was the temporary capital of Australia. The front steps are the obvious spot, but they can be crowded with wedding parties, tour groups and now and then a rally. This stand-here point is a calmer choice. Parliament Gardens is a small triangular garden beside the building, between Spring Street and Albert Street. From here you see the building from the side, with the garden's fountain and statues in the foreground. It makes a quieter, more relaxed frame than the straight-on view. If you want the classic view as well, walk round to the front for the columns looking down Bourke Street. Check for events before you go, as they can block your shots.
text.geographic_location: Parliament House stands on Spring Street, at the top of Bourke Street on the eastern edge of Melbourne's central grid. Parliament Gardens is the small triangular garden next to it, between Spring Street and Albert Street.
text.directions_text: Head for Spring Street, at the eastern end of Bourke Street on the edge of the city centre; by taxi or hired scooter, ask for Parliament House on Spring Street. Parliament Gardens is the small triangular garden beside the building, and it is a walkable stop between the Treasury and Parliament House. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the building seen from the side. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, statues and building together. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details such as the columns and stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Parliament Gardens (triangular garden beside the building, bounded by Spring Street and Albert Street). The Parliament building seen from the side and beside the garden's fountain and statues, a calmer frame than the front steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Put the fountain or a statue in the foreground and let the building fill the background. Turn on gridlines and keep the verticals of the columns straight. If the garden is busy, a tighter 2x frame on the facade avoids people. For the classic front view down Bourke Street, walk round to the steps or the top of Bourke Street. It is busier there, so be patient.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out the stonework. If you use ultra-wide, keep the building away from the edges of the frame, where it can look stretched.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light tends to flatter the stonework. Weekday daytimes can be busy with tour groups, so check for events before you go.

text.access_note: Parliament Gardens is a public garden, but access to the building itself, its steps and any tours can change, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Parliament Gardens is a public garden that visitors can normally walk into freely.
Soft morning or late-afternoon light generally suits stone buildings.
Weekday daytimes can be busier with tour groups.

name: St Paul's Cathedral, Melbourne
label: St Paul's Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Federation Square' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Federation Square' (way/1098427843): middle (358 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/13127644: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Saint Paul's Cathedral' (98 m across).
notes: Gothic Revival cathedral with tall spires across from Flinders Street Station.

text.description:
St Paul's Cathedral is the Anglican cathedral of Melbourne, and it sits right in the middle of the city on a busy corner with trams passing. The building was designed by the English architect William Butterfield and finished in 1891. The tall spires came later, built to a different design between 1926 and 1932. The central Moorhouse Spire reaches about 95 m. The site also marks where the first Christian service in Melbourne was held, in 1835.

It photographs well because the pointed spires and detailed stonework rise above a busy street scene. From the edge of Federation Square you look across the intersection of Flinders and Swanston Streets and can fit the facade, the spires and passing trams into one frame. Overhead tram wires, trees and power lines can clutter the view, so take a few shots from slightly different spots rather than relying on one. A second option is Princes Bridge, which gives a long view up Swanston Street towards the spires, with the tram lines leading your eye to the cathedral.

Stay on the footpaths and never stand on tram tracks or at tram stops.
text.geographic_location: In the centre of Melbourne, on the eastern corner of Swanston and Flinders Streets. It is diagonally opposite Flinders Street station and directly across Flinders Street from Federation Square.
text.directions_text: Head for Federation Square in the centre of Melbourne. The cathedral is across Flinders Street to the north-west, about 170 m away. Cross only at the signalled crossings, and watch for trams. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the facade, the spires and the street with its trams. Then try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the spires and stonework and to leave out some of the wires. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of street in the frame. It will make the spires lean and look smaller.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Federation Square (edge of the square facing the Flinders and Swanston Streets intersection). The cathedral's spires and facade seen across the busy intersection, with the street and trams in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the spires with a vertical line so they don't lean. Place the facade in the upper part of the frame and let a tram or the street fill the lower part. Move a few steps left or right to find a gap in the wires and trees. For a different view, walk to Princes Bridge and shoot up the bridge towards the spires, using the tram lines to lead the eye.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the sky or the stonework to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky stays blue and the detail in the stone shows. If a tram passes through the frame, a Live Photo lets you pick the best moment afterwards.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time when the street is not too busy and the light is soft. Overcast or low-sun conditions help avoid harsh shadows on the stonework.

text.access_note: The outside can be photographed from public footpaths and the square. Photography inside needs a permit from the cathedral shop and is not allowed during services or possibly weddings, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Soft light from an overcast sky or a low sun is kinder to stonework than harsh midday sun.
Telephoto lenses (2x-5x) can help leave out some of the overhead wires from the frame.
